card.title: Motion of a Satellite — Orbital Velocity and Time Period

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: A satellite orbits when gravity supplies the centripetal force: v₀ = √(GM/r) and T = 2π√(r³/GM). Energy is K = GMm/2r, U = −GMm/r, E = −GMm/2r. Orbital speed is mass-independent; higher orbits are slower but longer-period. Weightlessness arises from continuous free fall.

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Orbital velocity: v₀ = √(GM/r)
Near-surface orbital speed: v₀ = √(gR)
Time period: T = 2πr/v₀ = 2π√(r³/GM)

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Orbital Velocity Derivation:** $v_0 = \sqrt{GM/r}$ comes from equating gravitational force to centripetal force: $GMm/r^2 = mv_0^2/r$. This applies to *circular* orbits around a spherically symmetric mass. The satellite's mass cancels out — all satellites at the same radius have the same speed.  ·  **Period Law:** $T = 2\pi\sqrt{r^3/GM}$ is Kepler's third law for circular orbits. Squaring gives $T^2 \propto r^3$, independent of satellite mass. This is valid only for bound circular/elliptical orbits — not for escape trajectories ($E \ge 0$).

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: r is measured from the centre of Earth: r = R + h, never forget to add the radius.  ·  Orbital speed is ~7.9 km/s at the surface, 7.66 km/s at the ISS altitude, 3.08 km/s at geostationary.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: LEO speed: v = √(gR) = √(9.8×6.4×10⁶) ≈ 7.9 km/s.  ·  ISS period ≈ 93 minutes at r = 6.8×10⁶ m.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: ❌ 'A satellite must be above the atmosphere to feel no gravity.' ✅ A satellite feels gravity at every altitude — it is in continuous free fall. It never falls to Earth because its forward speed curves its fall into an orbit.  ·  ❌ 'Weightlessness means g = 0 on the ISS.' ✅ g at 400 km is ≈ 8.7 m/s² (89% of surface). Astronauts float because both they and the station accelerate toward Earth together (free fall).

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Derive v₀ = √(GM/r) and T = 2π√(r³/GM).  ·  Compute v and T for a satellite at a given altitude (R + h).

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Near surface: v₀ = √(gR) ≈ 7.9 km/s — remember this anchor value.  ·  T applet: for the ISS (≈ 90 min) confirm with T = 2π√(r³/GM).

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: A satellite orbits at 200 km above Earth. Find its orbital speed and period.  ·  Find the height at which a satellite has an orbital period of 2 hours.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Deriving v₀ and T from equating gravity to centripetal force is a year-on-year question.  ·  Finding the altitude for a given period (e.g., 2 h, 24 h) is a standard numerical.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Orbital velocity v₀ = √(GM/r) follows from gravity = centripetal force.  ·  Period T = 2π√(r³/GM) — Kepler's third law.  ·  Orbital speed is independent of satellite mass.  ·  Energy: K = GMm/2r, U = −GMm/r, E = −GMm/2r.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: v₀ = √(GM/r) — orbital speed depends only on radius, not satellite mass.  ·  T = 2π√(r³/GM) — Kepler's third law: T² ∝ r³.  ·  Higher orbit → slower speed, longer period.  ·  E_total = −GMm/2r: bound orbit, with K = −U/2.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: The first artificial satellite, Sputnik 1, launched in 1957, orbited at ~8 km/s — exactly the value predicted by v₀ = √(GM/r).  ·  Arthur C. Clarke proposed the geostationary orbit in 1945; it is now so crowded that slot allocation is internationally regulated.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: A satellite of mass 1000 kg orbits at r = 7×10⁶ m. Compute K, U and E.  ·  Why is a satellite's orbital speed independent of its mass?  ·  Show that T² ∝ r³ (Kepler's third law) from the orbit equations.

rows.label: More hints
rows.text: Energy numericals (K, U, E) for a given orbit are frequently asked.  ·  Conceptual: 'why do astronauts float?' — answer free fall.

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: Geostationary altitude ≈ 35,800 km; v ≈ 3.08 km/s.  ·  Moon period ≈ 27.3 days from T = 2π√(r³/GM).

rows.text: The orbital velocity of a satellite is given by: → B  ·  The period of a satellite in orbit is: → B

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **Orbital velocity (v₀):** a satellite stays in a circular orbit when the gravitational pull GMm/r² provides the required centripetal force mv²/r. Equating: GMm/r² = mv₀²/r → v₀ = √(GM/r). Near Earth's surface, v₀ = √(gR) ≈ 7.9 km/s.  ·  **Why v₀ matters:** too slow → the satellite spirals in; too fast → it escapes to a higher ellipse. The orbital speed depends only on the radius (GM/r), not on the satellite's mass — heavy and light satellites share the same orbit speed.  ·  **Time period (T):** T = circumference/velocity = 2πr/v₀ = 2π√(r³/GM) — Kepler's third law. Squaring: T² ∝ r³. A higher orbit has a longer period: the Moon (r ≈ 3.84×10⁸ m) takes ~27.3 days; the ISS (r ≈ 6.8×10⁶ m) takes ~92 minutes.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Weightlessness = free fall.  ·  Kinetic energy: K = GMm/2r  ·  Total energy: E = −GMm/2r (E = U/2, K = −U/2)

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **Energy Relations:** For circular orbits: $K = GMm/2r$, $U = -GMm/r$, $E = -GMm/2r$. Notice $K = -U/2$ and $E = U/2$. The negative total energy confirms a bound orbit. To raise an orbit, you ADD energy (thrust), but the orbital speed *decreases* because $v_0 \propto 1/\sqrt{r}$.  ·  Astronauts float because of free fall, not absence of gravity.  ·  ❌ 'Heavier satellites orbit slower.' ✅ Orbital speed is independent of the satellite's mass: v₀ = √(GM/r).

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ 'Higher orbit → faster speed.' ✅ Higher orbit means SLOWER speed (v₀ = √(GM/r)) but a LONGER period. To reach a higher orbit you must speed up at launch; once there, the circular speed is lower.  ·  ❌ 'T is proportional to r.' ✅ T ∝ r^{3/2} — the period grows faster than the radius.  ·  ❌ 'A satellite's kinetic energy increases as it moves to a higher orbit.' ✅ KE = GMm/2r DECREASES with height; the added energy is stored as potential energy (+GmM·Δ(1/r)) making the total E = −GMm/2r less negative.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Energy check at r = 7×10⁶ m, m = 500 kg: E = −GMm/2r ≈ −1.42×10¹⁰ J.  ·  E is negative everywhere in orbit — a positive total energy means escape.  ·  To compare orbits always compute r = R + h first.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: NEB asks to derive v₀ and T and to solve for altitude given T.  ·  r = R + h — always measure from the centre of Earth.  ·  v₀ = √(GM/r) is mass-independent: all satellites at the same height have the same speed.
